stemMd: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: It follows a technology from its invention through to the range of uses it has found around the world.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It introduces a method, reports the expectation the method's designer began with, and then explains why the results overturned that expectation.

options.label: C
options.textMd: It sets out a long-running scientific debate and then takes the side of one of the two camps.

options.label: D
options.textMd: It lists several ways of supplying water to dry regions and ranks them by the cost of installing each.

explanationMd:
Structure questions are answered by the shape of the text, not by its subject. Label each sentence with the job it does and the shape appears.

Sentences one and two set up the site and describe the method: mesh nets, gutter, tank. Sentence three gives Belmont's starting expectation and her reason for it, that a denser mesh would intercept more droplets. Sentence four reports the opposite outcome. Sentences five and six explain the mechanism behind that outcome and give the coarse mesh's better result. Method, expectation, reversal and explanation of the reversal is the option that names a method, the designer's opening expectation and the results that overturned it.

Check by testing each option against a feature the text would have to contain. A debate needs two named positions, a ranking by cost needs costs, and a history needs dates and a spread of users. None of the three appears anywhere in the passage.

distractorRationale.c: No debate is described. Only one researcher appears, and the disagreement in the passage is between Belmont's own expectation and her own results, not between two camps of scientists.
distractorRationale.d: Only one water-supply method is described, and the passage mentions no prices, budgets or installation costs of any kind, so nothing in it is ranked by cost.
distractorRationale.a: The passage gives no invention date, no history and no other users. It reports one researcher's nets on one ridge, not a technology's spread around the world.

accessibilityText: Using the passage about Nadia Belmont's fog-collecting nets, choose the description that best matches the passage's overall organisation.

provenance.notes: Original item. Each distractor names a structure that would require a feature the passage demonstrably lacks (a second position, costs, a timeline).

review.author: digital-sat-wave4-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The text introduces the net method, gives Belmont's initial reasoning that a denser mesh would catch more, then reports that those nets performed worst and explains why (air was blocked). A, C and D describe content the passage lacks: history of global uses, a two-camp debate, or a cost ranking.

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: Sentence-by-sentence: method, designer's expectation and reason, contrary result, mechanism and better result. That is D exactly. A needs two positions, B needs costs, C needs a timeline and worldwide use; none is in the text. Not published: awaiting a blind independent solve by a second party. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
